name: The Byzantine Empire
title: Social Hierarchy of the Byzantine Empire: From Emperor to Enslaved
period: c. 850–1204 (the middle Byzantine period, from the Macedonian emperors to the Fourth Crusade)

tiers.name: The emperor
tiers.you: You are God’s chosen emperor and the living law, at the centre of a great court, but no law secures your throne, and a successful rebel could blind you or send you to a monastery.
tiers.kid: The emperor ruled from a great palace in Constantinople, and people believed God had chosen him.
tiers.rise: Any man the army, Senate and people accepted could rule, and outsiders did: Basil I, born to peasant parents, rose from groom to co-emperor and seized sole power in 867, and Romanos I Lekapenos, a peasant’s son and admiral, was crowned in 920.
tiers.why: The emperor (basileus) was held to be chosen by God and to be the living law (nomos empsychos), and his court, whose ceremonies Constantine VII had set down in the Book of Ceremonies, was meant to mirror the order of…

tiers.name: The powerful
tiers.you: You hold a high court title and a command or an office, with estates worked by tenants, but your family’s standing depends on the emperor’s favour.
tiers.kid: Rich families held the top jobs in the army and government, but they needed the emperor’s favour.
tiers.rise: Imperial favour, office and marriage made a family great, and the emperor could raise men of any birth. Rebellion could ruin it: after the revolts of Bardas Skleros and Bardas Phokas, Basil II sidelined the old military families.
tiers.why: At the top of society stood “the powerful” (dynatoi), a legal term for the senior ranks of civil, military and church office, who usually also owned great estates.

tiers.name: The patriarch and bishops
tiers.you: You govern a diocese and its lands, rank in law among “the powerful”, and as a bishop you may not marry.
tiers.kid: Bishops led the Church in each region, and the patriarch of Constantinople was the most senior bishop in the empire.
tiers.rise: Bishops came from the monks and the educated clergy, so learning could carry a man of modest birth to high church office, but a patriarch who crossed the emperor could be deposed.
tiers.why: The Church of the empire was led by the patriarch of Constantinople, who crowned emperors, though emperors could also depose a patriarch, as Leo VI deposed Nicholas I Mystikos for opposing his fourth marriage.

tiers.name: Officials
tiers.you: You hold a court title and work in one of the great bureaus of Constantinople, dressed in the costume of your rank, and your career depends on the emperor’s grant.
tiers.kid: Officials kept the records, collected taxes and ran the empire’s offices for the emperor.
tiers.rise: Education in law and letters and a patron at court opened the way into the bureaus, and promotion came by the emperor’s grant; a change of emperor could end a career.
tiers.why: The empire was governed by a large, literate bureaucracy: in Constantinople there were hundreds, if not thousands, of officials at any time.

tiers.name: Soldiers
tiers.you: Your family holds land registered for military service; you serve with your theme’s army when called, with pay on campaign, and your household is spared most taxes.
tiers.kid: Many soldiers were farmers whose land came with a duty to serve in the army when called.
tiers.rise: The duty was hereditary and passed with the land. The army offered careers to provincials, and a successful general could seize the throne, as Nikephoros II Phokas did in 963.
tiers.why: Many peasant households in the themes, the military provinces, held land registered for military service (stratiotika ktemata).

tiers.name: Monks, nuns and parish clergy
tiers.you: You live in a monastery under its rule, keeping the round of prayer and work, or serve a village church as a priest who may be married.
tiers.kid: Monks and nuns lived in monasteries to pray and work, and many monasteries owned large farms.
tiers.rise: People of every rank, from deposed emperors to villagers, entered monasteries, and since bishops had to be celibate, learned monks were the natural candidates for high church office.
tiers.why: Monasteries ranged from small houses to great foundations in Constantinople and on Mount Athos, where the monk Athanasios founded the Great Lavra in 963 with the support of Nikephoros Phokas, turning a land of hermits…

tiers.name: Merchants and craftsmen of the guilds
tiers.you: You belong to one of Constantinople’s guilds, which fixes your prices, your profit and even the part of the city where you may trade, under the eye of the eparch.
tiers.kid: In Constantinople, bakers, silk makers and other traders belonged to guilds that set their prices.
tiers.rise: Entry to a guild needed its members’ election and a fee, which kept many out; outside the guilds, poor townspeople worked for wages.
tiers.why: Constantinople, with perhaps 400,000 to 500,000 people around 1200, was by far the largest city of the empire, and its trades were organised in guilds.

tiers.name: Free peasants
tiers.you: You own your fields in a village whose families answer for the land tax together, and the emperor’s laws protect you from the powerful, though a bad harvest could force you to sell.
tiers.kid: Many farmers owned small fields in villages and paid taxes to the emperor.
tiers.rise: A free peasant could prosper and buy land or send a son into the army or the Church, but debt or a bad harvest could force him to sell and become a tenant (paroikos) on a great estate.
tiers.why: Most Byzantines were peasants, and in the 10th century free smallholders, who owned their land and lived in village communities, were the main pillar of society and of the state’s revenue.

tiers.name: Dependent peasants
tiers.you: You farm land that belongs to a great landowner or a monastery and pay him rent and dues, but your plot passes to your children and you cannot be removed while you pay.
tiers.kid: Many farmers worked land that belonged to rich landowners or monasteries and paid them rent.
tiers.rise: Tenancy passed from parents to children, so most families of paroikoi stayed tenants for generations; free smallholders sank into it through debt or by selling their land to the powerful.
tiers.why: Paroikoi were peasants who farmed land they did not own, as tenants on the estates of great landowners, monasteries, churches and the emperor himself.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You belong to a master, most likely in a rich town household; the law forbids him to kill you, but your children will be born slaves, and before 1095 you cannot legally marry.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and made to work without pay, mostly as servants in rich homes.
tiers.rise: Freedom came by manumission, and under Justinian’s law a freed slave became a citizen; Manuel I Komnenos freed all the slaves of Constantinople in the 12th century.
